item.research_question: How can process parameters be optimized to minimize and align surface roughness (Ra and Rz) on curvilinear titanium alloy surfaces regardless of the surface shape and tilted angle?
item.processing_route: Turning of spherical curvilinear surfaces (radius of curvature R = 14 mm, length L = 10 mm) using a CNC machine with interpolated axes, sintered carbide insert (N123F1–0318–R0S05F), cutting edge radius rε = 1.588 mm, and variable feed rates (f) and cutting speeds (vc)
item.test_conditions: Tilted surface angles δ ranging from ±17° to 0°; feed rates varied across 3 levels; cutting speed varied across 3 levels; depth of cut ap = 0.7 mm (case study); measurement via Talysurf Intra 50 profilometer (ISO 4287/ISO25178 standards)
key_findings: Cutting speed has an insignificant effect on surface roughness parameters (p = 0.531 for Ra and p = 0.355 for Rz).
Feed rate and tilted surface angle are the most influential parameters on surface roughness (Ra and Rz).
The optimized method achieved surface roughness parameters below upper limits (Ra ≤ 0.63 μm and Rz ≤ 3.2 μm) across the full range of tilted angles.
Machining time with optimized feed rate was 160 s, compared to 304 s required for a constant minimum feed rate (fmin = 0.03 mm/rev) to achieve the same roughness alignment.
The optimized feed rate range was 0.03–0.115 mm/rev, whereas a constant feed rate of 0.085 mm/rev only yielded acceptable roughness for tilted angles between −1° and 12°.
The regression equations for roughness prediction were simplified to depend only on feed rate and tilted angle due to the lack of cutting speed effect.
item.mechanism: The authors explain that during turning of curvilinear surfaces, the change in the undeformed chip area shape and the modification of angles between the cutting insert flank face and the work surface cause variable surface roughness. By approximating the curved contour with elementary straight lines and developing regression models based on experimental data, they can calculate specific feed rates for each surface segment to maintain aligned roughness values.
item.limitations: The study notes that the proposed method relies on a simplification of approximating curved contour sections by elementary straight lines, though geometrical analysis confirmed the insignificant effect of this simplification on the contour shape and undeformed chip area. Additionally, the current model does not account for cutting depth, radius of surface curvature, tool wear, or total cutting force components.
item.future_work: The authors plan to modify the proposed method to apply a new calculation method based on a neural network to provide more accurate prediction of surface roughness parameters and to include the impact of additional cutting data such as cutting depth, radius of surface curvature, tool wear, and total cutting force components.
quotes: The results analysis of the experiment showed the significant effect of the feed rate f and the tilted angle of surface δ on the surface roughness.
The machining time when applying a constant feed rate f = 0.085 mm/rev is 120 s.
In the future, the authors plan a modification of the proposed method to apply the new calculation method based on a neural network.

records.text: Paper card. Question: How can process parameters be optimized to minimize and align surface roughness (Ra and Rz) on curvilinear titanium alloy surfaces regardless of the surface shape and tilted angle?. System: Ti6Al4V titanium alloy (annealed at 750 °C). Processing: Turning of spherical curvilinear surfaces (radius of curvature R = 14 mm, length L = 10 mm) using a CNC machine with interpolated axes, sintered carbide insert (N123F1–0318–R0S05F), cutting edge radius rε = 1.588 mm, and variable feed rates (f) and cutting speeds (vc). Test conditions: Tilted surface angles δ ranging from ±17° to 0°; feed rates varied across 3 levels; cutting speed varied across 3 levels; depth of cut ap = 0.7 mm (case study); measurement via Talysurf Intra 50 profilometer (ISO 4287/ISO25178 standards). Findings: Cutting speed has an insignificant effect on surface roughness parameters (p = 0.531 for Ra and p = 0.355 for Rz).; Feed rate and tilted surface angle are the most influential parameters on surface roughness (Ra and Rz).; The optimized method achieved surface roughness parameters below upper limits (Ra ≤ 0.63 μm and Rz ≤ 3.2 μm) across the full range of tilted angles.; Machining time with optimized feed rate was 160 s, compared to 304 s required for a constant minimum feed rate (fmin = 0.03 mm/rev) to achieve the same roughness alignment.; The optimized feed rate range was 0.03–0.115 mm/rev, whereas a constant feed rate of 0.085 mm/rev only yielded acceptable roughness for tilted angles between −1° and 12°.; The regression equations for roughness prediction were simplified to depend only on feed rate and tilted angle due to the lack of cutting speed effect.. Mechanism: The authors explain that during turning of curvilinear surfaces, the change in the undeformed chip area shape and the modification of angles between the cutting insert flank face and the work surface cause variable surface roughness. By approximating the curved contour with elementary straight lines and developing regression models based on experimental data, they can calculate specific feed rates for each surface segment to maintain aligned roughness values.. Limitations: The study notes that the proposed method relies on a simplification of approximating curved contour sections by elementary straight lines, though geometrical analysis confirmed the insignificant effect of this simplification on the contour shape and undeformed chip area. Additionally, the current model does not account for cutting depth, radius of surface curvature, tool wear, or total cutting force components.. Future work: The authors plan to modify the proposed method to apply a new calculation method based on a neural network to provide more accurate prediction of surface roughness parameters and to include the impact of additional cutting data such as cutting depth, radius of surface curvature, tool wear, and total cutting force components..
